items.prompt: Which statement accurately describes ordinary hash-table lookup complexity without overclaiming?

options.text: Worst-case O(1) for every key distribution and implementation.
Always O(log n) because the table must search a balanced tree.
Expected O(1) under ordinary distribution assumptions, with O(n) worst case possible for n stored keys.

feedback.reason: Hash lookup is commonly described as expected O(1), while a linear worst case remains possible unless stronger guarantees are specified.

blocks.text: Complexity claims must name their model. With well-distributed hashes and controlled load, expected lookup examines a constant amount of state. If many keys collide or the implementation’s defenses do not supply a stronger bound, a lookup may inspect O(n) entries. The exact worst-case guarantee is implementation- and threat-model-dependent.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.worst_constant: Collisions or implementation-specific adversarial cases can force many stored entries to be examined; constant time is not a universal worst-case guarantee.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_logarithmic: Ordinary hash tables do not inherently perform a balanced-tree search for every lookup; expected access is commonly constant under stated assumptions.

items.prompt: An algorithm processes n fixed-width keys and performs two expected O(1) hash operations per key. It stores at most n keys. Classify expected total time and extra space.

feedback.reason: A constant expected amount of hash work is repeated n times, and retained state can grow with n.

blocks.text: The scan executes at most 2n hash operations. Under the prompt's expected-O(1) operation model, 2n · O(1) = O(n) expected total time. The table holds at most n fixed-width key entries, so its worst input-size extra space is O(n).

items: Time O(1) mistakes one operation's cost for the cost of n iterations, and O(log n) is too small for a scan that may inspect every key.
Time O(n log n) would require logarithmic work per key, while O(n²) would require linear work per key; neither follows from expected-constant hashing.
Space O(1) or O(log n) cannot retain n distinct entries, while O(n²) exceeds the maximum one entry per processed key.

blocks.title: Model boundary
blocks.text: The time result is expected or amortized under well-distributed hashing and geometric resizing; it is not a deterministic worst-case claim.

constraints: Assume fixed-width keys and an ordinary well-distributed resizable hash table.

items.prompt: A resizable hash table grows capacity by a constant factor, such as doubling, when a load threshold is reached. A rebuild can make one insertion cost O(n). Which conclusion is justified over a long sequence of insertions?

options.text: Every insertion is O(n) because some insertion triggers a rebuild.
The resizing component of insertion can still be amortized O(1) because expensive rebuilds are spread across many operations.
Rebuilding costs O(1) because hashing is constant time.

feedback.reason: Occasional linear rebuilds are compatible with amortized constant insertion when the resizing schedule provides enough cheap operations between rebuilds.

blocks.text: Amortized analysis bounds the whole sequence rather than every insertion separately. With capacities 1, 2, 4, … up to N, the rebuild work is 1 + 2 + 4 + … < 2N = O(N). Adding N ordinary insertions keeps total work O(N), so average amortized cost is O(1) per insertion. A resize-triggering insertion can still take O(N); the conclusion depends on the stated geometric growth.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.every_insert_linear: A worst cost for an occasional operation does not imply that every operation pays that cost; amortized analysis distributes it across the sequence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.rebuild_free: Rebuilding must revisit and place existing entries, so its direct cost grows with the number of stored keys.

items.prompt: An algorithm processes n strings of length m. Each iteration hashes the entire current string and performs one expected O(1) table lookup after the hash is computed. Classify expected time and extra space if all n strings may be retained as keys.

feedback.reason: Hashing each length-m key costs O(m), so key processing dominates expected constant table access.

blocks.text: Hashing one string reads m characters, so n strings require n · O(m) = O(nm) hashing work. The n expected-O(1) table operations add O(n), which is no larger. Under the stated accounting convention, retaining n keys of m characters each requires O(nm) extra space.

items: Time O(n) ignores key length, while O(n + m) hashes only one length-m string instead of n such strings.
Time O(nm log m) would include sorting each string, which is not performed, and O(n²) invents pairwise string processing.
Space O(1), O(n), and O(m) each omit at least one growing dimension of n retained length-m key contents.

blocks.title: Storage convention
blocks.text: If an implementation retained only references to caller-owned immutable strings, internal table storage could be O(n); this item explicitly counts the retained key content, making it O(nm).

constraints: Assume hashing reads all m characters.
Count retained key content as extra space for this item.

items.prompt: A system requires a deterministic O(log n) or better worst-case lookup guarantee for attacker-controlled keys. Which conclusion is safest?

options.text: Any hash map automatically provides worst-case O(1), so no implementation detail matters.
Replacing the map with a set creates the required worst-case guarantee.
Do not rely on a generic expected-O(1) hash claim; choose an implementation with a documented worst-case bound or an ordered alternative.

feedback.reason: A worst-case requirement must be satisfied by a documented data-structure guarantee, not by an expected hash-table heuristic.

blocks.text: Algorithm analysis often accepts expected O(1) hashing, but adversarial inputs change the required evidence. An ordered tree can provide O(log n) worst-case operations, or a hardened hash implementation may document stronger behavior. The choice must be based on actual guarantees and key model, not container name.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.generic_hash_enough: Expected performance under ordinary distribution is not the deterministic worst-case guarantee required by the threat model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.set_instead_of_map: Set and map often share the same underlying hash behavior; changing payload semantics does not strengthen collision guarantees.

items.prompt: A set and a map use the same hash-table implementation and therefore have similar expected key-operation complexity. Which statement remains true?

options.text: They are interchangeable for every algorithm because their expected complexity is similar.
The map can preserve a payload such as count or index, while the set preserves membership only.
The set implicitly preserves exact counts for repeated insertions.

feedback.reason: Complexity equivalence does not erase the semantic difference between membership and key-to-value association.

blocks.text: Choosing between set and map is first an information decision. Only after both candidates are semantically valid should cost and memory decide among them. A count map, index map, and grouping map can share the same expected lookup class while supporting materially different algorithms.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.interchangeable: Similar asymptotic access cost does not make two representations encode the same information or invariant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.set_has_counts: Repeated insertion of the same key leaves one membership entry and does not expose multiplicity.

items.prompt: A seen set and a frequency map both take expected O(n) time over n fixed-width inputs. Why can the frequency map still be necessary?

options.text: The map is asymptotically faster than the set.
Only the set has collision worst cases; the map is worst-case constant.
The output distinguishes multiplicities, which the set does not preserve.

feedback.reason: Equal expected runtime does not make presence and multiplicity equivalent; the required answer determines the payload.

blocks.text: Both algorithms may execute one hash operation per input element, but they compute different functions. The set returns membership information; the frequency map retains counts. Complexity analysis can compare valid strategies, but it cannot justify discarding information the output requires.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.map_faster: Under the same implementation assumptions, both commonly have the same expected aggregate time class.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.set_worst_linear_map_constant: Sets and maps can share the same collision behavior; payload type does not remove worst cases.

items.prompt: A developer argues that inserting before checking is harmless because both operations are expected O(1). What is the flaw?

options.text: Lookup is always asymptotically more expensive than insertion.
Operation order changes the state invariant and may allow the current occurrence to satisfy a prior-occurrence check; equal cost does not make the orders equivalent.
Hash algorithms must never insert before any check.

feedback.reason: Complexity describes resource cost, while operation order determines which occurrences and state transitions are semantically visible.

blocks.text: In duplicate or complement lookup, the table must represent earlier elements when checked, so insertion first can create a false self-match. In grouping, creating a bucket before appending is appropriate because existence is not evidence of a prior member. Expected O(1) for both operations says nothing about this distinction.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.check_more_expensive: Both operations may share expected cost; the issue is what state each operation observes, not an asymptotic difference.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.insert_never_allowed: Initialization-before-use is correct in grouping and other workflows; order depends on the invariant, not a universal prohibition.

items.prompt: If hashing a key costs O(m) for key length m and n keys have lengths m1,...,mn, what total hash-work bound should be stated?

options.text: O(m1 + m2 + ... + mn) for hashing, plus table-operation overhead; O(n) applies only when key length is fixed.
O(n) because each hash lookup is one abstract operation regardless of key length.
O(max mi) because only the longest key is hashed.
O((sum mi)^2) because hashing always compares every key with every other key.

feedback.reason: Hashing cost includes reading the key; fixed-width O(1) assumptions do not transfer to variable-length strings for free.

blocks.text: A table lookup may be expected O(1) after hashing, but computing n variable-length hashes costs the sum of key lengths. Retained key storage also includes those characters, not only n pointer-sized entries.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n_only: O(1) hash-table operations can hide O(m) key hashing work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.max_only: Every key is processed, not just the longest.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.square_lengths: Ordinary hashing does not require all-pairs key comparison under its assumptions.

items.prompt: Two hash maps store the same n distinct keys, but one stores only presence and the other stores a list of all original indices per key. What complexity distinction matters?

options.text: The one-to-many payload can require Θ(n) additional provenance storage and output work even when key lookup remains expected O(1).
They have identical space because the hash keys are identical.
A list payload is constant-size because the map has one entry per distinct key.
Storing indices necessarily changes each hash lookup to expected O(n²).

feedback.reason: Hash-key operation complexity and payload size are separate; preserving occurrence identity can dominate memory and output costs.

blocks.text: A presence set stores one record per distinct key. A map from key to all indices stores a total number of index entries proportional to the input, potentially plus output records. Expected lookup may remain constant per key, but enumerating a payload costs its size.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_everything: Payload cardinality changes even when key cardinality is the same.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.map_payload_constant: A bucket can contain many occurrences.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.lookup_becomes_n2: Payload size affects retrieval/output work, not necessarily the hash lookup itself.

items.prompt: What auxiliary space does a hash set of up to n distinct input keys typically use?

options.text: O(n), because it stores up to n key entries.
O(1), because each lookup is constant time.
O(log n), because hashing creates a balanced tree.
O(n²), because every pair of keys is stored.

feedback.reason: Time complexity and storage complexity describe different resources.

blocks.text: Expected O(1) lookup does not mean constant memory. A set or map grows with the number of retained keys or payloads.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant_space: Constant lookup time is not constant storage.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.log_space: A hash table is not defined by logarithmic key storage.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.quadratic_space: One entry per distinct key is sufficient, not one per pair.

items.prompt: What can happen when many distinct keys collide in the same hash bucket?

options.text: Lookup can degrade toward linear behavior in the number of colliding entries, depending on the implementation.
Collisions delete all keys from the table.
The input becomes sorted automatically.
Collisions cannot affect worst-case lookup time.

feedback.reason: Hashing narrows a lookup to a bucket; collision resolution still has to inspect candidates inside it.

blocks.text: Expected constant-time claims assume a suitable distribution and implementation behavior. Worst-case analysis must account for adversarial or pathological collisions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_input: Bucket placement does not sort keys.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant_worst: A collision-heavy bucket can require many comparisons.

items.prompt: If a map stores each key together with a long list of associated indices, what changes in the complexity analysis?

options.text: Space must include the total number of stored payload entries, not only the number of distinct keys.
Payload length never affects space because hashing stores only keys.
Appending and iterating payloads are always O(1) regardless of list length.
Payloads force all keys to be sorted first.

feedback.reason: The map owns both key entries and their associated data.

blocks.text: State complexity against the required output: storing one earliest index per key is different from storing every occurrence index for all keys.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.keys_only: Payload lists occupy memory and can dominate it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.time_free: Operations over a payload list scale with its length.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_required: Hash storage does not require sorting.

items.prompt: What is the main asymptotic contrast between expected hash lookup and comparison sorting for n items?

options.text: A hash-based pass is often expected O(n), while comparison sorting is typically O(n log n).
Both are always O(1) for n items.
Hashing is always O(n log n) and sorting always O(n).
Both require no auxiliary state.

feedback.reason: Hash membership trades ordering for expected direct lookup, while comparison sorting establishes global order.

blocks.text: This comparison is conditional: hashing has distribution and memory assumptions, and sorting may be the right choice when ordered output or deterministic worst-case behavior matters.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_constant: Processing n items cannot generally be constant time.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_nlogn_sort_linear: The usual expected comparison is the reverse.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_space_zero: Both approaches need storage or in-place state under their contracts.
